Content:
Suppose we are given the function

Content:
[MATH: y=5\log_6(x-2).]

Content:
How do we plot its graph?

Content:
As usual, we can do this by combining transformations of the curve [MATH: y=\log_6 x.]

Content:
- We start with the graph of [MATH: y=\log_6 x{:}]

[IMG: /graphics/bdb0c6b259d1a9aa682f127b1f1aa0cf]
- Translate it by [MATH: 2] units to the right to get the graph of [MATH: y=\log_6{(x-2)}.]

[IMG: /graphics/aa3a3e5426fe73d31f40282bb5142c17]

Notice that points [MATH: (1,0)] and [MATH: (6,1)] on the graph of [MATH: y=\log_6 x] map to the points [MATH: (3,0)] and [MATH: (8,1)] on the graph of [MATH: y=\log_6 (x-2),] respectively.
- Then, stretch the result by a scale factor of [MATH: 5] parallel to the [MATH: y]-axis to get the graph of [MATH: y=5\log_6{(x-2)}.]

[IMG: /graphics/15cfecf1f7090b9961119eb5dfb0902c]

Content:
So, to plot the curve of a transformed logarithmic function, we apply subsequent transformations presented in the given function, as usual.

sections.normalized_html:
The graph of [MATH: y=k\log_2 {x}] can be obtained from [MATH: y=\log_2 {x}] by a vertical stretch of scale factor [MATH: k.]

From the diagram, we deduce that under such a transformation, the point [MATH: (4,2)] that lies on [MATH: y=\log_2 {x}] becomes

[MATH: (4,k \cdot 2)=\left(4,3\right)]

which lies on [MATH: y=k\log_2 {x}.]

Therefore, [MATH: k=\dfrac 32.]

items.title: Finding Unknown Parameters Given a Transformed Logarithmic Function

sections.normalized_html: The diagram below shows the graph of [MATH: y=k \log_5 (bx).] Find the value of [MATH: b\cdot k.]
sections.readable_text:
The diagram below shows the graph of [MATH: y=k \log_5 (bx).] Find the value of [MATH: b\cdot k.]

[IMG: /graphics/9c65b77cb64a1cbf796399b4bf72797a]

sections.normalized_html:
Clearly, [MATH: b \neq 0.] Substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac1b] into the equation of the curve, we get

[MATH: y|= k\log_{5} (b ⋅ (1)/(b)); = k\log_{5} 1; = 0.]

So, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac1b, 0\right)] lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that [MATH: (2,0)] lies on the curve. Hence,

[MATH: (2,0) = \left(\dfrac1b,0\right)\quad\Rightarrow\quad b=\dfrac12.]

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point [MATH: (10,3)] into the equation:

[MATH: k\log_{5} (bx)|= y; k\log_{5} ((1)/(2)x)|= y; k\log_{5} ((1)/(2) ⋅ 10)|= 3; k\log_{5} 5|= 3; k|= 3]

Finally,

[MATH: b\cdot k = \dfrac12 \cdot 3 = \dfrac32.]

Item 11 — Example: Finding Unknown Parameters Given a Transformed Logarithmic Function

Example Prompt:
The diagram below shows the graph of [MATH: y=k \log_5 (bx).] Find the value of [MATH: b\cdot k.]

[IMG: /graphics/9c65b77cb64a1cbf796399b4bf72797a]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Clearly, [MATH: b \neq 0.] Substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac1b] into the equation of the curve, we get

[MATH: y|= k\log_{5} (b ⋅ (1)/(b)); = k\log_{5} 1; = 0.]

So, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac1b, 0\right)] lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that [MATH: (2,0)] lies on the curve. Hence,

[MATH: (2,0) = \left(\dfrac1b,0\right)\quad\Rightarrow\quad b=\dfrac12.]

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point [MATH: (10,3)] into the equation:

[MATH: k\log_{5} (bx)|= y; k\log_{5} ((1)/(2)x)|= y; k\log_{5} ((1)/(2) ⋅ 10)|= 3; k\log_{5} 5|= 3; k|= 3]

Finally,

[MATH: b\cdot k = \dfrac12 \cdot 3 = \dfrac32.]
